deviations: The token comes only from the process environment (AGENT111_DAEMON_TOKEN). There is no --daemon-token flag: passing one is a clear startup error, because argv is readable by every local user. The env file is not read for it either: the token is minted per spawn, so a copy in a file would be stale and a secret at rest. This matches the README amendment wording "reads the token from the environment". The brief said "env/flags", so this is narrower than the brief.

The daemon URL guard is stricter than the model-base guard. It accepts only http:// with a loopback IP literal (127.0.0.0/8 or [::1]); `localhost` and other hostnames are refused, as are userinfo, query and fragment. A non-loopback URL refuses startup, like the model base. Reason: 111d redirects Host: localhost (308), and the bearer must never follow a redirect. The client also disables redirects (max_redirects 0) and the environment proxy, because ureq 3 reads HTTP_PROXY by default.

A malformed token (not hex, or more than 256 characters) is a startup error that never echoes the value. I chose this over quietly treating it as missing, to match how other bad config values are handled. node111 always mints 64 hex characters.

messages.send checks the recipient with 111d (GET /contacts/{to}) before writing anything. A non-contact (404), a pending message request, or a mismatched node_id means no proposal is written. With no token, a 401, or an unreachable daemon, it answers "unavailable" and also writes nothing. The spec does not cover this; I picked the fail-closed reading.

The proposal carries `to` and `text` in its body, not in structured fields. Adding a field such as `message: {to, text}` would mean changing store.rs::Proposal and save_proposal, which this task does not own. The body contract F2 must parse is exactly `"to: " + <64 lowercase hex> + "\n\n" + <text verbatim>`. The title is `Send a message to <alias or label>`. If the lead prefers a structured field, it is an additive change to store.rs; the daemon already ignores extra fields.

Incoming message text (dir other than `own`) is labelled too: it is handed over as `untrusted_text`, and the result carries a notice saying so. The spec only requires the untrusted block for nearby.read. I added this as extra protection because message requests come from strangers.

messages.read `limit` is required, as the spec shape lists it without `?`. It is clamped to 1–50, below the API's 500, to keep tool results small enough for model context. contacts.read returns at most 100 contacts and 100 requests; nearby.read returns at most 50 nodes, with heard/shown counts.

deviations: The identify profile is a restart policy whose first exit is final: meshmud::identify_backoff(), crash_loop_threshold = 1. Why: under the normal 2 s back-off, a meshmud that exits within the 50 ms poll window is respawned before identify notices, which means a second open of the port. A child's policy cannot be swapped in place without editing supervise.rs, which this task does not own. So if the identify-born service child exits later, the monitor replaces it on its next tick with a meshmud under the service policy. That is the same single respawn the service policy would make, and the claims stay with `meshmud` the whole time.

Added MeshtasticConfig.dev_root (production is `/`). The serial-uplink presence check (`uplink lost`) looks for the path under this root, so tests can point it at the fake /dev tree. meshmud itself always opens the real path.

registry.rs: an absent store entry with no last_record_summary used to be deleted on the next tick, which silently dropped its Meshtastic binding. An entry that holds a binding is now kept, because a binding is configuration (for example, a Wi-Fi board bound by address is never detected).
The identify route runs the step in a spawned task. Why: if the client disconnected mid-probe, the request future was dropped and meshmud kept running with the port claimed by `identify:<id>`.
Facts.meshmud.channel_utilization is always null. The reader excludes the local board from its file, so 111d has no board-reported value. Nodes' own utilization is still in Nearby.

GET /api/v1/fromradio returns exactly one frame per call, whatever `all=` says. The firmware's all=true concatenates protobufs with no delimiters, so we never do that; the client polls until it gets an empty answer.

There is no route that binds a Wi-Fi board by address. The registry never detects Wi-Fi boards, so identify has no target for one. M1 does render and run a TCP binding found in devices.json (tested on a phone). The openapi identify text says 'USB or Wi-Fi board'; the address-binding path needs an agent or Layer 6 task.

A board whose binding exists but whose meshmud binary is missing reports child Absent with board set. The registry rules in services/mod.rs (not mine) then read this as `meshtastic_unbound` ('identified but not set up'), when it should say 'meshmud not installed'. Suggested fix: add an installed flag or reason in services/mod.rs.

Identifying a second board while one is bound returns 409 port_busy on the downlink, because there is one meshmud and one 127.0.0.1:11230 downlink. The user must forget the first board before identifying another.

Presence hygiene beyond the spec: 111d deletes fabric/presence/meshtastic.json when a board is unbound and before it spawns the reader, and reads the file only while a board is bound. This fails closed: an old or foreign node DB can never make the service read LIVE.

deviations: The localhost 308 on the main listener skips /health and /api/status. These are Layer 1 machine contracts: tests/dashboard_http.rs pins GET /api/status with Host localhost:11180 -> 200, and curl does not follow redirects by default. Every other path, including /api/v1/*, gets the 308 to http://127.0.0.1[:port]<path?query>. [::1] is matched bracketed and served as is. The Host guard runs before the redirect.

Origin check is stricter than §13. The spec asks for the Origin/Referer authority check on non-GET, WebSocket upgrades and SSE opens only when Sec-Fetch-* is absent. I enforce it whenever the request is one of those kinds; a panel's own JS is same-origin, so nothing legitimate is refused. Also fail closed: an unknown Sec-Fetch-Site value is refused like cross-site, TRACE and CONNECT are refused like OPTIONS, and a missing or repeated Host is refused.

What 'enabled' means (spec left it implicit; I picked the fail-closed reading): the panel is registered, its bundle directory <root>/current/<bundle> exists, and the registry's published state for its service is anything but `unset`. Only enabled panels get a listener. Minting for a panel that is not enabled answers 404 not_found, matching the contract's 'or its service is not set up'.

Without a valid p111_<id> cookie and without a ticket, a panel request answers 401 unauthenticated. §13 only defines 403 panel_ticket_expired, which is kept for spent, expired, unknown, wrong-peer or wrong-panel tickets. A ticket presented with a non-GET method is burned and answered 403. The successful swap is a 303 to entry.path with Cache-Control no-store.

Trusted-loopback mints are bound to the current pair code (a hash of it, held in the session record) rather than an s111 session. `111 dashboard rotate` changes the code, so those sessions are revoked. The automatic pair-code rotation after 20 failed pair attempts also revokes them (fail closed).

LAN-off revocation happens at daemon start, because LAN sharing is read once per start. When the daemon starts with LAN off, every panel session minted while LAN was on, or from a non-loopback peer, is dropped.

The mint endpoint has two extra refusals: 400 when the dashboard Host cannot address a panel, and 403 loopback_only (an existing contract code) for a loopback-only panel requested from a non-loopback dashboard host, since that ticket URL could never work.
With a valid session, an Upgrade request answers 400: there is no WebSocket in v1. A manifest declaring [proxy] websocket/sse = true is never registered.

Manifest strictness: [frame] sandbox accepts only "default" and [license] served only "unmodified". A [health] url is accepted only as a loopback http URL with multi_client = true, and v1 does not probe it (health reads unknown).
Panel listeners also bind [::1]:<port> best effort, exactly as the dashboard does. A failed IPv4 bind is retried after 30 s (BIND_RETRY).

daemon/mod.rs is shared with M1; I made no edits to it this session. Its panel wiring (ShimRegistry -> PanelHost::load -> insert_ext -> sources.panels = panels::provider -> panels::spawn) is from the previous run. M1 added meshtastic.attach_panels(&panel_host), which forwards revocations to the shim's close_session and calls host.report_dropped every tick. api_v1/mod.rs carries `pub mod panels;` and `.merge(panels::router())` next to M1's nearby registration; both are kept.
result.notes:
I resumed from the crash. All the on-disk P1 work compiled and was kept. The only missing piece was tests/api_v1_panels.rs, which was not on disk or in any scratchpad, so I wrote it fresh (12 integration tests, all passing). The source files only went through rustfmt this session; their logic is unchanged.

Suggested reading order:
1. panels/mod.rs (module doc, then `PanelHost`): what 'enabled' means, slots in state/panels.json, `reconcile`, `frame_origins`, the provider and `spawn`.
2. panels/listener.rs: the request pipeline doc at the top, then `respond` / `swap` / `dispatch`, then the serve loop with header-read and idle timeouts and a connection cap.
3. guard.rs and ticket.rs (`Binding`, `binding_alive`, `SessionStore` with its 0600 file and revocation broadcast).
4. headers.rs (response policy; also holds the reserved-proxy cookie rules, `filter_upstream_set_cookie` / `strip_request_cookies`, as the proxy seam) and static.rs (SPA fallback never under /api).
5. routes.rs diff (per-request `dashboard_csp`, `localhost_redirect`), then api_v1/panels.rs.

The tests cover every item in the row: ticket flow, spent ticket and re-mint, cookie-present ticket spent, expiry, peer binding, cross-site refused with no CORS headers, the Host/Origin matrix including the localhost 308, header rewrite, SPA vs API paths (shim keyed by session, 502 upstream_error, 413 body cap, panel without a shim), CSP per host, loopback-only binding with LAN on, untrusted loopback (Termux) still needing the ticket, and revocation on rotate, logout, disable and LAN-off.

Open questions and nits:
(a) On trusted loopback, the agent's bearer token can also mint panel tickets, because it counts as the implicit loopback session. Is that acceptable?
(b) If a panel is disabled and re-enabled before its old listener task drops the socket, the rebind fails and retries 30 s later.
(c) Static files are read and hashed whole for each ETag, with no cache (64 MiB cap). Fine for v1.
(d) `headers::redact_ticket` exists, but no panel code logs a URI at all, so it is never called.
(e) The main dashboard listener still has no header-read or idle timeouts. That predates this task, and §13 requires them on panel listeners.
(f) The full check.sh cannot be green until U1 lands: the notices stage fails on U1's pnpm-lock.yaml change and the UI stage is expected red. M1's api_v1_meshtastic shim test is timing-flaky (failed 2 of 4 runs).

deviations: §6.1 ACK ordering is applied as selection priority: the acknowledged packet's range/partial first, then current epoch newest-first, then frozen, ≤ 8. The wire order is C2's canonical ascending order, because ack.rs rejects any other order. A frozen epoch's prefix travels as the range [1, prefix].

ENROLL_OK starts with a status byte: 0 OK (card + custody_seq_floor follow), 1 mismatch, 2 refused, 3 locked out. The kind registry has no ENROLL_REJECT, so refusals answer on the same kind (mailbox.rs). The spec only says `ENROLL_OK {hub card, custody_seq_floor}`.

Custody rejects keep `sent` with a reason. REJECT_UNKNOWN_DEST maps to `hub_not_yours`, which the C1 contract describes as a queued reason; it is the closest code to §9's "your hub does not know them". REJECT_UNENROLLED maps to `not_enrolled`, which is not in C1's emitted set, so clients render `unknown`. C1/U1 may want to grow the enum.

send() during RestoreFloorRequired returns FabricError::RestorePending: Store::queue_own_message refuses to allocate an n, so nothing can be stored. The contract says POST /messages is always 202. F2 must map this error, or the contract text changes. Messages queued before the floor show queued + restore_pending, nothing is sealed (ACKs/control included), and the next fabric event re-mints.

§5 planning MTU is the current route's MTU (hub route minus the 120 B custody wrap), else the smallest registered link MTU, else 160 B. Links with MTU ≥ 4096 keep a 512 B reserve for the INTRO card, a piggybacked ACK and the custody wrap. So a tcp-lan-only node with no path yet plans for tcp-lan rather than 160 B.

Window policy: fresh fragments first, then retransmissions, ≤ 16 outstanding per peer, Tier-0 packets included. Under retransmit-first, one sender's window caps the receiver at 16 partials, so the store's eviction could never trigger from a single sender. Fresh-first is also how the >16-partials test reaches eviction.

`node1…` contacts still waiting for their card live in memory: the contacts table requires key material. They are rebuilt at start from outbox peers with no contact. Known effect: a forgotten contact with undelivered messages reappears as a key-less contact after a restart. A store column would fix this (C3 follow-up). Read marks (ContactPatch.read_seq) are also in memory only (no column).
The startup complete_partials path delivers as kind MSG, because rx_frags stores no kind (C3 schema). v1 senders only fragment MSG.
Message requests use the store's `requests` table; the contacts.request column is unused. Adding a pending requester's card out of band counts as accepting the request.
Fail-closed reading of §7.2(3) 'INTRO is tcp-lan-only': a receiver drops an INTRO arriving on a non-tcp-lan link (mailbox items are still accepted) and zeroizes the provisional pair key.

Stricter than §8.1's attribution list: hub replies (CUSTODY_ACK, ENROLL_OK, MAILBOX_ITEM streams) go only on a connection attributed to the requester. A node's own traffic goes only on a connection attributed to the peer, or on one it dialed itself where the first announce named the peer. An inbound unattributed connection gets nothing.

A member commits its mailbox cursor past every item it processed, including one its range list deferred. The hub keeps the item evict-first, and the sender retransmits directly when the two meet. ACKs sent through the hub are fire-and-forget.

The fabric does not bind the tcp-lan listener. F2 calls TcpLan::listen according to FabricSettings.listen_lan / hub_role, and the fabric emits FabricEvent::Settings for F2 to persist (enrollment sets home_hub). FabricSettings is the fabric's in-memory copy of fabric/settings.
tcp_lan accept loop: on an accept() error (e.g. EMFILE) it now pauses 100 ms instead of spinning. This is a transport detail, like keepalive and reconnect back-off.

Events are emitted before any API command runs inside a tick, so an API reply never precedes the events describing the state it reports. Coalescing per message per tick otherwise holds; `change` is the first change in the tick.

result.notes:
Read first: the fabric.rs module doc (design, what attribution gates, readings), then the frag.rs doc section 'SACK semantics after a receiver evicts a partial', then tests/hub_flow.rs.

Partial-eviction decision (the KNOWN SEMANTIC): both halves are implemented.
1. The receiver rebuilds every ACK's partial list from rx_snapshot, so an evicted partial is never claimed again.
2. The sender applies a listed partial with replace semantics: bits it had SACKed but the listing omits are regressed and resent. An unlisted message is left alone, because small-MTU ACKs are truncated.
SACK bits live in memory (TxTracker), because outbox.acked is sticky. After a restart, everything unacknowledged is resent once and the receiver re-ACKs it (DuplicateFragment). Proof test: lossy.rs `more_than_16_partials_evicted_and_recovered` checks Bob holds exactly partials n=5..=20 after eviction, at least 4 bits regressed, and all 20 messages delivered exactly once.

Design: one actor per node owns the store, the connections and the sender/receiver state. Inputs are link frames, LinkEvents (Fabric::link_events() sink; Fabric::gate() is the AnnounceGate backed by the contacts cache) and API jobs. Each tick flushes owed ACKs (piggybacked when they fit), mailbox commits and pumps, writes frames, then emits coalesced events. There are no timers. Retries are driven by link events, contact events, ACK evidence (loss inferred from SACKs of later-sent fragments), Fabric::retry and Fabric::retry_all; retry_all is the daemon's 'fabric event' and also re-fetches from the hub and re-asks for cards. The typed API is threads, thread, message, send, cancel (tombstone), retry, retry_all, contacts CRUD (add by card / by node1, patch accept/alias/pin/read, forget), card, status, enroll, offer, dismiss_offer, settings, patch_settings, with_store, shutdown, abort.

Tests (14 integration plus unit tests in the F1 modules), all from the brief:
- tests/hub_flow.rs:
  - queued→sent→relayed→delivered, checked through the event stream
  - REJECT_UNKNOWN_DEST shown as sent + hub_not_yours
  - node1 card request answered by the hub, plus INTRO through the mailbox held as a request
  - REJECT_FULL → mailbox_full, then recovered
  - hub abort and restart on the same port, resumed from the cursor (exactly 2 items above it)
  - replayed announce and replayed sealed packet on fresh raw sockets: no sealed frame ever pushed, only Alice attributed, stale counter rises
  - sender crash with a new epoch: the direct new-epoch packet arrives first, the older epoch from custody is delivered frozen, each message exactly once
- tests/lossy.rs:
  - Tier 1 at 160 B with 15% loss and 15% reorder both ways: at most 16 outstanding, retransmits > 0
  - eviction recovery
  - duplicates re-ACKed, never redelivered
  - a 9th isolated range is deferred, and every retransmitted duplicate is acknowledged
  - restore_pending
  - INTRO refused on a non-tcp-lan link
- tests/requests.rs:
  - INTRO request: ignore (no ACK, even on retry), then accept (ACK); reply
  - request quota 0 and store_full refusals: dropped without an ACK, counted, provisional key zeroized
  - ACK piggybacked on queued data
- The unit test outbox.rs `ack_ordering_rule_selects_the_acknowledged_range_first` covers more than 8 ranges across epochs.

Observation for C3 (not my file): once, under 12 concurrent test processes, Store::open failed in two tests of the same process at the same instant with SQLCipher's 'An error occurred with PRAGMA key or rekey'. It looks like a first-use init race in SQLCipher/OpenSSL. A dedicated probe (16 concurrent first opens × 180 runs, with and without contention) did not reproduce it. The test harness now serializes Store::open per process. The daemon opens one store per process, so production should be unaffected, but it is worth a look.

Wishes for other owners:
- C3 store: a newest-N messages query (threads()/thread() currently scan a peer's whole history through messages_with); columns for node1-pending contacts and read marks; a kind column in rx_frags.
- C1 contract: decide the reason codes for custody rejects while `sent`, and the restore_pending behaviour of POST /messages.

Open questions:
- Should send() to a still-pending requester be refused, instead of queued as waiting_for_key until accepted?
- Should enroll() carry its own bound? It has none (no timers); the F2 route must time it out.
